opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core reason is that right now there's a real asymmetry in who gets to put knowledge *into* a model. If you're one of a handful of big labs, you decide what goes into pretraining and post-training, and everyone else mostly interacts with the model from the outside, through prompting, retrieval, stuffing things into the context window. Those are great tools, and I use them all the time, but they have limits. Context is expensive, it's temporary, and the model doesn't really *internalize* anything. Every conversation it starts from scratch.

Training, especially efficient fine-tuning, changes that. It lets a hospital, a small company, or a single researcher take a model and teach it their domain: their codebase, their internal vocabulary, their data, the way they reason about problems. The knowledge lives in the weights, so it's there every time, not just when you remember to paste it in.

What makes it compelling to me as a researcher is that we don't fully understand it yet. When I worked on comparing low-rank fine-tuning with full fine-tuning, one of the striking things was the tradeoff. Some methods are cheap and preserve what the model already knows, but they learn less of the new material. Others absorb more but can overwrite existing capabilities. That learning-versus-forgetting tension is the central scientific question if you want ordinary people to safely add knowledge to models.

So I see training as a democratizing tool, but one that needs better science and better infrastructure. If we can make it reliable, predictable, and cheap, so you can add knowledge without breaking what's already there, then "customize your model" becomes as normal as "fine-tune your search index" or "set up a database." That's when a lot more people get to shape what these systems actually know.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts training with prompting, retrieval, and adding material to context, explaining that those approaches are temporary while training makes knowledge persist in the model.

r002.rationale: It argues that training could let ordinary people and smaller organizations shape models, but does not connect that opportunity to benefits pursued in high-stakes technical domains.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that I came to this from a place of frustration with how much of the capability in these models stays locked behind one specific recipe.

Right now, the way most people get new knowledge into a model is through the context window. You retrieve some documents, you stuff them into the prompt, and you hope the model reads them well. And that works surprisingly often. But it's fundamentally a rental arrangement. The model doesn't actually know anything new after the conversation ends. You pay the cost of re-reading those documents every single time, and the model's reasoning over them is shallow in a way that's hard to articulate until you compare it to what happens when something is actually in the weights.

When you train, you're doing something different in kind. You're changing what the model is, not just what it's looking at. A model that has been trained on your codebase, or your clinical protocols, or your company's decade of internal decisions, doesn't just retrieve facts about them. It develops intuitions. It knows which things tend to go together, what the exceptions look like, what an expert in that domain would find obvious. That's the thing I find compelling. Training is the mechanism by which models move from being well-read generalists to being colleagues who have actually lived in your problem.

The reason I say "more people" specifically is that right now this is a capability concentrated in a handful of labs. If you want a model that deeply understands your domain, you mostly can't get one, because the process of training is expensive, fragile, and requires a kind of institutional knowledge that very few teams have. I think that's a temporary state of affairs, and I think it's worth working hard to make it temporary. There's an enormous amount of specialized human knowledge out in the world that will never make it into a pretraining corpus, in hospitals, in manufacturing floors, in legal practices, in small research groups. The only way that knowledge becomes something a model can act on fluently is if the people who have it can train on it themselves.

So I see it less as a technical preference and more as a question about who gets to shape these systems. If training stays a lab-only activity, the models learn what labs think is important. If it becomes something a broad range of people can do, the models start to reflect a much wider slice of what humans actually know.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts repeatedly retrieving documents through the context window with training that changes the model and gives it deeper domain intuitions, presenting training as a stronger way to integrate knowledge.

r002.rationale: It points to specialized knowledge in hospitals, manufacturing, legal practices, and small research groups, and argues that training should become accessible to a broad range of people rather than remain concentrated in a few labs.

astra-6.text:
I think what’s compelling is that training lets you do work once that can then help a lot of people in very different situations. You can put a new capability into a model, and people can draw on it when they’re learning something, solving a problem, or trying to do work they couldn’t do before.

And there’s a difference between making information available and making it useful. You can have access to a great explanation and still not know how it connects to what you’re doing. A model can help bridge that gap: you can ask follow-up questions, try an example, and get help at the point where you’re stuck. That’s the possibility that excites me—making knowledge easier for people to actually use.

r001.rationale: The response says training can add a capability once and help many people, but it does not compare that approach with manually curating learning resources.

r002.rationale: The response describes benefits for many people in varied situations, but does not connect them to training in high-stakes technical domains.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what’s compelling is the gap between having knowledge available and being able to use it. You can put information on the internet, but someone still has to find it, understand it, and figure out how it applies to their situation. Those are substantial barriers.

Model training offers a way to make that knowledge more accessible through interaction. Someone can ask a question in their own words, get an explanation at the right level, try something, and get feedback. That can help turn information into a capability they can actually use.

And the scale is exciting. If you improve a model’s ability to explain something or help someone work through a problem, that improvement can reach many people. The important question is whether they come away better able to do something they care about.

r001.rationale: The response says model interaction can make knowledge more accessible, but it does not compare this with manually curating learning resources or call it superior.

r002.rationale: The response says model improvements can reach many people, but it does not mention benefits from high-stakes technical domains being extended to a broader population.
